scenes.heading: Data Compliance
scenes.narration: Data compliance is the practice of handling data in accordance with laws and regulations such as GDPR, CCPA, and HIPAA, turning legal duties into concrete engineering controls.

scenes.heading: Key obligations
bullets: Consent and lawful basis for collection
Data subject rights: access and erasure
scenes.narration: Compliance requires a lawful basis and, often, explicit consent before collecting personal data. It grants individuals rights to access, correct, and erase their data, which your systems must be able to fulfill. It demands data minimization and purpose limitation, so you collect only what you need and use it only for stated purposes. And it imposes rules on where data may reside, how long it may be kept, and how quickly a breach must be reported.

scenes.heading: Handling a right-to-erasure request
scenes.narration: When a verified erasure request arrives, you first use lineage and a catalog to locate every place that subject's data lives. You then delete or irreversibly anonymize those records across all operational and analytical stores. Because copies propagate, you must also address backups and downstream derived datasets, often via tombstones or scheduled purges. Finally you record documented proof that the request was fulfilled, which regulators may later require as evidence.

scenes.heading: PII vs sensitive special-category data

right.label: Special category
points: Frequently must be encrypted or masked

scenes.narration: Ordinary personal data like names, emails, and device identifiers must be protected, but pseudonymization and access controls are often sufficient. Special-category data such as health records, biometrics, and ethnicity carries stricter requirements, typically demanding explicit consent, tighter access, and stronger technical safeguards. Classifying data correctly is the foundation, because you cannot apply the right controls or honor rights requests if you do not know which fields are personal or sensitive.

scenes.heading: Engineering controls for compliance
bullets: Retention policies that expire old data
Consent flags that gate downstream use
Audit logs that prove what happened
scenes.narration: Compliance becomes real through concrete engineering controls. Classifying data automatically at ingestion tags personal and sensitive fields so policies can act on them. Retention policies automatically expire or purge data once its lawful retention period ends, so you do not keep data longer than allowed. Consent flags travel with records and gate whether downstream jobs may use them for a given purpose. And comprehensive audit logs provide the evidence regulators require to prove how data was handled.

scenes.text: Bake compliance into the pipeline as classification, lineage, and retention controls, not as a bolt-on audit at the end.
scenes.narration: Treat compliance as an engineering property built into the pipeline through data classification, lineage, and automated retention controls, rather than as a bolt-on audit performed after the fact.
